summary: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery limits how long a router may wait between Router Advertisements and how long its lifetime can be, but allows link-specific documents to override them. This document allows those limits to be changed per link.

plainLanguage.summary: A router tells neighbors it is still around. This lets the timing be adjusted for each connection instead of being the same everywhere.

questions: how to change maximum router lifetime in ipv6
what is the maximum router lifetime in ipv6
how often are ipv6 router advertisements sent
what does rfc 8319 change in rfc 4861
subtitle: Lets IPv6 routers announce themselves much less often on links where multicast is costly, by raising two Neighbor Discovery limits to 65535 seconds.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery caps how long a router may wait between unsolicited multicast Router Advertisements and how long its lifetime can be. On links where multicast is costly, those caps force more multicast traffic than necessary.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8319 updates RFC 4861 to raise three limits (Router Lifetime, MaxRtrAdvInterval and AdvDefaultLifetime) to 65535 seconds, and gives guidance on how the lifetime and the interval should relate.
tldr.outcome: Links without native multicast can send far fewer Router Advertisements. Legacy hosts may mishandle a lifetime above 9000 seconds, and sparse advertisements make rogue ones more harmful.

today: RFC 8319 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2018. It updates RFC 4861, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why the Old Limits Hurt
sections.content:
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery relies on IP multicast, expecting that it uses bandwidth efficiently and avoids interrupting network nodes. On some data link layers, multicast is not natively supported. On such links, any reduction in multicast traffic is highly beneficial.

The fixed constants in RFC 4861 make it hard to relax the multicast timers. Link-specific documents already exist that tune Neighbor Discovery constants for certain systems, for example RFC 6459 and RFC 7066 for 3GPP cellular links.

This document updates RFC 4861 to increase the maximum time allowed between unsolicited multicast Router Advertisements (RAs) from a router interface, and to increase the maximum router lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: Some roads make it very costly to shout to everyone at once. The old rule said routers had to shout fairly often. This RFC lets them shout less often on those roads.

sections.title: Interval Versus Lifetime
sections.content:
MaxRtrAdvInterval is an upper bound on the time between two successive Router Advertisements. AdvDefaultLifetime says how long a host may keep the router as a default router. The RFC compares them with a ratio K = AdvDefaultLifetime / MaxRtrAdvInterval, which tells how many advertisements are guaranteed to be sent before the router lifetime expires.

On a theoretically perfect link with no losses, K just above 1 would be enough. On real links that lose packets, K should be greater than 2 so that a single lost advertisement does not make the router entry expire.
sections.plainLanguage: If a note says "I'll be back within an hour" and you only write a note every hour, one lost note leaves everyone worried. Writing several notes per promise makes losing one harmless.

sections.title: Choosing K and the Hard Rule
sections.content:
As an example, assume a ballpark 1% probability of packet loss. Then K = 2 gives a 0.01% chance of an outage due to a packet loss, and K = 3 gives 0.0001%. In reliability terms, K ~= 1 gives 99%, K ~= 2 gives 99.99%, and K ~= 3 gives 99.9999%.

With higher loss, or if more reliability is wanted, K can be higher still. Some data link layers deliver reliably at Layer 2, so a K just above 1 may be considered there. Because the choice does not affect interoperability, the RFC imposes no specific constraint beyond one rule: AdvDefaultLifetime MUST be greater than or equal to the selected MaxRtrAdvInterval. Otherwise the router lifetime is guaranteed to expire before the next RA can be sent, creating an outage.
sections.plainLanguage: Each extra note you send makes it less likely that everyone misses all of them. The one firm rule is that your promise must last at least as long as the gap between notes.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 4861
sections.content:
The RFC updates Sections 4.2 and 6.2.1 of RFC 4861 with three edits, all to 65535 seconds:

  • In Section 4.2, the paragraph defining Router Lifetime: 9000 becomes 65535 seconds.
  • In Section 6.2.1, the paragraph defining MaxRtrAdvInterval: 1800 becomes 65535 seconds.
  • In Section 6.2.1, the paragraph defining AdvDefaultLifetime: 9000 becomes 65535 seconds.

The probability of packet loss must be considered when choosing the relationship between the two variables, as explained in the previous section.
sections.plainLanguage: Three numbers on a rulebook page are crossed out and replaced with a much bigger one, 65535 seconds.

sections.title: Host Behavior and Legacy Hosts
sections.content: Legacy hosts on a link with updated routers may have trouble with a Router Lifetime of more than 9000 seconds. The authors tested a few implementations on general-purpose operating systems and saw no problem with values above 9000. Still, some implementations might wrongly reject such RAs, even though RFC 4861 requires receivers to handle any value.
sections.plainLanguage: Older gadgets might not expect such a long promise and could get confused, even though the rules say they should cope.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: On a link where Router Advertisements are few and far between, the harm done by a rogue router sending an unsolicited RA is greatly increased. The RFC points to approaches such as RA-Guard (RFC 6105) and SEcure Neighbor Discovery, or SEND (RFC 3971), to prevent rogue RAs. It has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: If the real announcer speaks rarely, a fake announcer who speaks up is believed for a long time. Guards and secret handshakes help keep fakes out.
